headline: Ram Island Granite on the Ebb: Bass Working the Bunker Pods, Albies Still a Question Mark
subhead: Warm water has the boulder fields stacked with peanut bunker and sea bass, but the first albacore scout of the season hasn't shown itself yet — here's where the pieces are lining up.
body_markdown:
The peanut bunker are pushing tight against the granite this week, balled up in the current seams off Ram Island and along the north face of Wamphassuc Point, and that's telling you almost everything you need to know before you ever wet a line. When bait stacks that close to the rock, something's pushing it there, and this time of year in the Sound it's almost always a bass working the boulder edges on the moving tide. Fish the last two hours of the ebb around Ram Island's western ledges — the water pulls off the rock, bait gets pinned against the structure, and stripers slide up from the deeper holes to pick them off. A white or bunker-pattern Deceiver on an intermediate line, worked with a slow strip-strip-pause right along the rock face, has been the right call. Spinning guys are doing the same job with a 5-inch soft plastic paddletail on a 3/8-ounce jighead, cast up-current and let it swing down past the boulders like it's lost.

Water's warm right now — New London's reading 77.4°F, and the Sound east of Mystic tracks close to that number this time of year, warmer than the western basin around Kings Point at 74.8°F. That gradient matters. The bass haven't abandoned the rocks in this heat, but they've gone nocturnal and tide-dependent about it. Midday sun on slack water and the boulder fields go quiet — fish tuck into the shade lines between rocks and won't commit to anything moving fast. First light and the last hour before dark, working the outgoing around Stonington Breakwater and the rock piles off Wamphassuc, is where the quality fish are coming from. Nothing enormous being reported, but slot-class fish in the 26 to 32-inch range have been consistent enough on bunker chunks and swim shads worked slow along the breakwater's outer face.

Black sea bass have filled in nicely around the rock piles off Fishers Island and the deeper structure toward the Race side of the Sound. This is the pattern you lean on when the striper bite goes quiet in the heat of the day — anchor up on a known pile in 20 to 35 feet, drop a double-hook rig baited with squid strips or clam, and work it slow off bottom. The sea bass have been thick enough this week to keep rods bent while you wait out the tide change for the next bass push. Fluke are scattered through Little Narragansett Bay and the sandy pockets tight to the rock — not a banner fluke summer so far, but a 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with Gulp in white or pink, dragged along the sand-to-rock transition zones, has picked at a few keepers in the 18 to 20-inch class on the drift.

Now to the question everybody in this stretch is asking: where are the albies. We flagged this zone as one of the more likely early spots for false albacore scouting activity, and the water's doing its part — that steep thermal gradient across the Sound, the warm push out of New London, the general trend line toward the 70s that's already got Montauk and Block Island in play for the first bonito scouts of the season. But nothing's confirmed here yet. No boils reported off the breakwater, no bait getting bombed by anything fast and silver around Fishers Island. That's not unusual for the first week of August — the albies in this stretch typically don't show in numbers until the water settles into that mid-to-upper 60s range with a consistent bay anchovy and silverside push, and we're still running warmer and baitier than that classic albie trigger. Watch the temperature breaks along the Fishers Island side and the rip lines off Watch Hill closely over the next week or two. When those first fish show, they show fast and they show in the same spots year after year — the rip off Watch Hill Point, the drop-off east of Ram Island, and the current seam running off the outer breakwater.

Tautog fishing is in its usual summer lull — the rocks are holding fish, but the bite's sluggish in the warm water and most serious tog anglers in this zone are saving their effort for the fall push when temperatures drop back through the 60s and the fish get aggressive again on green crab. Not worth burning a tide on it right now unless you're fishing deep, shaded structure on the bottom stages of the tide.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if the wind stays out of the south and southwest and keeps this warm water pinned against the Connecticut shore. If a cold front pushes through and knocks New London back toward the low 70s, that's exactly the kind of temperature break that could trigger the first albie scouts of the season here — worth checking the breakwater and the Fishers Island rip lines the morning after any real wind shift. Until then, work the boulder fields on the tide changes for bass, lean on the sea bass piles through the heat of the day, and keep the fly rod rigged and ready. When the albies arrive in this stretch, there's rarely much warning.
